```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = NA, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 3.8)
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))
bca <- read_rds("data/bca262.rds")
```

## Two tibbles from deck 06

```{r}
#| label: data
avg_price <- bca |>
  group_by(act_use_cat, sale_year = year(sale_date)) |>
  summarise(avg_price = mean(price, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

van17 <- bca |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver", year(sale_date) == 2017) |>
  mutate(price_m = price / 1e6)
```

In deck 06, `ggplot()`, `aes()`, and `geom_*()` decided what is drawn. This deck covers the functions around them. A few of those change what a chart says, not only how it looks.

## scale_*() turns values into axes and colours

The name says what changes: `scale_`, the mapping, then how.

::: {.small}
| Function | Changes |
|---|---|
| `scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2000, 2010, 2020))` | Which x values get a gridline and a label |
| `scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 2000))` | The x-axis range, **dropping rows outside it** |
| `scale_x_log10()` | The x-axis, to a log scale |
| `scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2")` | The colours for the `colour` mapping |
:::

::: {.key-point}
When you review AI-written code, you can skim most `scale_*()` lines: they change labels and colours. Stop at `limits`, which drops rows, and log scales, which change what geoms compute.
:::

## Axis limits can remove data

`van17` holds City of Vancouver sales in 2017, with `price_m` in millions.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: limits
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.2
ggplot(van17, aes(floorarea, price_m)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 2000)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 5))
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: coord
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.2
ggplot(van17, aes(floorarea, price_m)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 2000),
                  ylim = c(0, 5))
```
:::
:::
::::

Left: `limits` dropped the `r sum(van17$floorarea > 2000, na.rm = TRUE)` homes over 2,000 sq ft **before** fitting the line. Right: `coord_cartesian()` only zooms.

## Log scales spread out skewed data

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: no-log
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.5
ggplot(van17, aes(floorarea, price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1)
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: log
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.5
ggplot(van17, aes(floorarea, price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar())
```
:::
:::
::::

Left: a few large, expensive homes stretch the axes, and most sales crowd into a corner. Right: on a log scale each gridline is a multiple of the last, so the spread shows.

`scales::label_dollar()` uses `label_dollar()` from the scales package without loading it. `label_comma()` and `label_percent()` work the same way.

::: {.notes}
- `label_number(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M")` writes 2,000,000 as 2M. Decks 09 and 11 use it.
- A log scale transforms the data before geoms compute. `geom_smooth(method = "lm")` on these axes fits log price on log floor area, a different line from the one on the original axes.
:::

## Bars start at zero

::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: sf-bars
van_sf <- bca |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver", act_use_cat == "S/F Res",
         between(year(sale_date), 2021, 2025)) |>
  group_by(year = year(sale_date)) |>
  summarise(median_price = median(price, na.rm = TRUE))
sf_bars <- ggplot(van_sf, aes(year, median_price)) + geom_col()
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: sf-bars-numbers
#| include: false
p22 <- van_sf$median_price[van_sf$year == 2022]
p25 <- van_sf$median_price[van_sf$year == 2025]
# coord_cartesian() pads the limits by 5% of the range on each side
y_bottom <- 2e6 - 0.05 * (2.3e6 - 2e6)
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: sf-bars-full
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 1.8
sf_bars +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 2.3e6))
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: sf-bars-zoom
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 1.8
sf_bars +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(2e6, 2.3e6))
```
:::
:::
::::

A bar's length shows its value. On the right, the 2022 bar is `r round((p22 - y_bottom) / (p25 - y_bottom), 1)` times as long as the 2025 bar, but the median fell only `r round(100 * (1 - p25 / p22))`%. To zoom in, use points or a line.

::: {.notes}
- `scale_y_continuous(limits = c(2e6, 2.3e6))` would remove every bar instead: each bar starts at 0, outside the limits.
- AI tools often zoom bar charts "to show the differences". Ask for points or a line instead.
:::

## Which day do sales happen?

```{r}
#| label: weekday
#| fig-height: 2.4
bca25 <- bca |>
  filter(year(sale_date) == 2025) |>
  mutate(day = wday(sale_date, label = TRUE))

ggplot(bca25, aes(x = day)) + geom_bar()
```

The days are in calendar order. How does ggplot know that Mon comes after Sun?

```{r}
#| label: weekday-numbers
#| include: false
n_day <- \(d) sum(bca25$day == d)
```

::: {.notes}
- Also ask why weekends are almost empty: `r n_day("Sat")` sales on Saturdays and `r n_day("Sun")` on Sundays in 2025, out of `r format(nrow(bca25), big.mark = ",")`. Recent BC Assessment records use the conveyance date, when ownership transfers, and transfers are registered on business days. The date is not when the buyer agreed to buy.
- Thursday is the busiest day, with `r round(100 * n_day("Thu") / nrow(bca25))`% of sales. Ask for explanations; the data alone cannot settle them.
- Use one recent year for anything by day of the week. In 2005–2014, 18–24% of each year's sales fall on a weekend: those records come from an older source whose date definition is not documented.
- `label = TRUE` uses the computer's language, so a student whose system is set to French or Chinese sees day names in that language.
:::

## wday() returns a factor

```{r}
#| label: weekday-factor
class(bca25$day)
levels(bca25$day)
```

::: {.key-point}
A **factor** stores categories with a fixed order, its **levels**. ggplot draws bars, stacks, and legends in level order.
:::

::: {.notes}
"ordered" means the levels can be compared: Sun < Mon. Deck 09 comes back to it.
:::

## Text goes in alphabetical order

```{r}
#| label: weekday-text
#| fig-height: 2.4
ggplot(bca25, aes(x = as.character(day))) + geom_bar()
```

`as.character()` turns the factor into text, which has no levels. ggplot sorts text alphabetically.

## lubridate works with dates

`year()` has been in our code since deck 02. It comes from **lubridate**, which loads with the tidyverse.

::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: lubridate
d <- ymd("2025-03-14")
c(year(d), mday(d))
month(d, label = TRUE)
wday(d, label = TRUE, week_start = 1)
```
:::

`ymd()` reads text as a date. `week_start = 1` puts Monday first: the function sets the levels.

## The functions around the geoms

::: {.small}
| Family | Controls | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `scale_*()` | How values become axes and colours: limits, breaks, number formats, log scales | `scale_y_log10()` |
| `coord_*()` | The plotting area: zoom, flip | `coord_flip()` |
| `facet_*()` | One panel per group | `facet_wrap(~ act_use_cat)` |
| `labs()` | Text: title, axis names, legend title, caption | `labs(y = "Price")` |
| `theme_*()`, `theme()` | The look that is not data: background, fonts, legend position | `theme_minimal()` |
| `guides()` | Legends | `guides(colour = "none")` |
:::

Inside a geom, `alpha`, `linewidth`, and `position = "dodge"` set that layer's look. Use these names when you ask AI to restyle a chart; to sort bars by value, ask for `fct_reorder()`.

## Sales in four cities

```{r}
#| label: city-sales
cities <- c("City of Vancouver", "City of Surrey",
            "City of Burnaby", "City of Richmond")
city_sales <- bca |>
  filter(juris_label %in% cities, year(sale_date) <= 2025) |>
  count(juris_label, year = year(sale_date))
city_sales |> head(3)
```

`city_sales` has one row per city and year. `n` is the number of sales.

## facet_wrap() draws one panel per group

```{r}
#| label: facet
#| fig-height: 2.6
ggplot(city_sales, aes(year, n)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ juris_label, nrow = 1)
```

The panels share one y-axis, so heights compare across panels. Use facets when lines in one panel would overlap.

```{r}
#| label: richmond-numbers
#| include: false
drop_12 <- \(n) round(100 * (1 - n[2] / n[1]))
all_sales <- bca |> filter(year(sale_date) %in% 2011:2012) |> count(year(sale_date))
richmond <- city_sales |> filter(juris_label == "City of Richmond", year %in% 2011:2012)
```

::: {.notes}
- Richmond's 2012 dip is partly real and partly a gap in `bca262.rds`, whose 2012 records for Richmond and Delta are incomplete. Richmond's sales fell `r drop_12(richmond$n)`% from 2011, against `r drop_12(all_sales$n)`% across Metro Vancouver. Ask students what else could explain a sudden drop.
:::

## Free scales hide differences in level

```{r}
#| label: facet-free
#| fig-height: 2.6
ggplot(city_sales, aes(year, n)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ juris_label, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y")
```

```{r}
#| label: facet-numbers
#| include: false
sales25 <- city_sales |> filter(year == 2025)
n25 <- \(city) sales25$n[sales25$juris_label == city]
```

`scales = "free_y"` gives each panel its own y-axis. Shapes are easier to compare; levels are not. Burnaby's line now fills its panel like Surrey's, yet Surrey had `r round(n25("City of Surrey") / n25("City of Burnaby"), 1)` times as many sales in 2025. Read the axis labels before you compare panels.

## Bars stack by default

```{r}
#| label: stack-data
van_sales <- bca |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver",
         between(year(sale_date), 2015, 2025)) |>
  count(year = year(sale_date), act_use_cat)
sales_plot <- ggplot(van_sales, aes(year, n, fill = act_use_cat))
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: stack
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 1.8
sales_plot +
  geom_col()
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: dodge
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 1.8
sales_plot +
  geom_col(position = "dodge")
```
:::
:::
::::

Left: the stack shows totals, but the top segments start at different heights, so single-family sales are hard to compare. Right: `position = "dodge"` starts every bar at zero.

::: {.notes}
`act_use_cat` is text, so the legend and the stack follow alphabetical order. As a factor, they would follow its levels.
:::

## position = "fill" turns counts into shares

```{r}
#| label: fill
#| fig-height: 2
sales_plot +
  geom_col(position = "fill")
```

Each bar now sums to 1: shares, not counts. The axis still says `n`, and nothing warns you. Label it yourself:

```{r}
#| label: fill-labels
#| eval: false
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(y = "Share of sales")
```

## Quick check: shares or counts?

```{r}
#| label: quiz-numbers
#| include: false
van_wide <- van_sales |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = act_use_cat, values_from = n) |>
  mutate(strata_share = round(100 * `Strata Res` / (`Strata Res` + `S/F Res`)))
pick <- \(y, col) van_wide[[col]][van_wide$year == y]
```

On the last chart, strata's share of Vancouver sales rose from `r pick(2016, "strata_share")`% in 2016 to `r pick(2019, "strata_share")`% in 2019. Did the number of strata sales rise?

**A.** Yes  **B.** The chart cannot tell you

::: {.fragment}
**B.** A share can rise while the count falls. Strata sales fell from `r scales::comma(pick(2016, "Strata Res"))` to `r scales::comma(pick(2019, "Strata Res"))`, but single-family sales fell faster, from `r scales::comma(pick(2016, "S/F Res"))` to `r scales::comma(pick(2019, "S/F Res"))`. To compare counts, use `position = "dodge"`.
:::

## Read a long AI-written chart

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: ai-chart
#| eval: false
# 1. data and mappings
ggplot(avg_price,
       aes(sale_year, avg_price, colour = act_use_cat)) +
  # 2. what to draw
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  # 3. how values become labels and colours
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  # 4. text
  labs(title = "Average sale price",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  # 5. the look that is not data
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
```{r}
#| label: ai-chart-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
ggplot(avg_price,
       aes(sale_year, avg_price, colour = act_use_cat)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(title = "Average sale price",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
:::
::::

::: {.key-point}
Only `ggplot()`, `aes()`, and `geom_*()` decide what is drawn. Most other lines change only the look. The next slide lists the exceptions.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Order matters for themes: `theme(legend.position = "bottom") + theme_minimal()` silently resets the legend, because a complete theme replaces earlier `theme()` settings. Put `theme_minimal()` first.
- To learn what a line does, comment it out and run the chart again.
:::

## Lines that change what a chart says

::: {.small}
| Line | What it changes | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `scale_x_continuous(limits = ...)` | Drops rows before geoms compute | Zoom with `coord_cartesian()` |
| `scale_x_log10()`, `scale_y_log10()` | Geoms compute on the logs | Say "log scale" on the axis |
| `coord_cartesian(ylim = ...)` on bars | Bar lengths stop matching values | Start bars at zero |
| `facet_wrap(scales = "free_y")` | Each panel gets its own y-axis | Read the axis labels |
| `position = "fill"` | Counts become shares | Label the axis as a share |
:::

::: {.key-point}
When you review AI-written chart code, look for these lines first. Each changes what a chart says, and the chart still looks fine.
:::

## Practice: price trends by property type

For the City of Vancouver, plot the median sale price in each year from 2000 to 2025, with one line for each `act_use_cat`.

1. Summarise first: one row per year and property type.
2. Map `act_use_cat` to `colour`.
3. Show the prices in dollars on the y-axis.

## Answer

::: {.small}
```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: trend-practice
#| fig-height: 3
van_trend <- bca |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver", year(sale_date) <= 2025) |>
  group_by(year = year(sale_date), act_use_cat) |>
  summarise(median_price = median(price, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

trend_plot <- ggplot(van_trend, aes(year, median_price, colour = act_use_cat)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar())
trend_plot
```
:::

## Save a chart for your slides

```{r}
#| label: save
#| eval: false
ggsave("temp/van_trend.png", trend_plot, width = 8, height = 4.5)
```

::: {.key-point}
Save the chart in an object, then pass it to `ggsave()`. Use the PNG in PowerPoint or Google Slides.
:::

## Practice: strata's share of sales

For the four cities in `cities`, show strata's share of sales in each year from 2005 to 2025.

1. Count sales by city, year, and property type.
2. Draw bars of shares, one panel per city.
3. Label the y-axis as a share, in percent.
4. In which city did the strata share change most?

## Answer

::: {.small}
```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: share-practice
#| fig-height: 2.6
city_type <- bca |>
  filter(juris_label %in% cities, between(year(sale_date), 2005, 2025)) |>
  count(juris_label, year = year(sale_date), act_use_cat)

ggplot(city_type, aes(year, n, fill = act_use_cat)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  facet_wrap(~ juris_label, nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(y = "Share of sales", fill = NULL)
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: share-numbers
#| include: false
surrey <- city_type |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Surrey") |>
  mutate(share = round(100 * n / sum(n)), .by = year) |>
  filter(act_use_cat == "Strata Res")
s_share <- \(y) surrey$share[surrey$year == y]
```

::: {.notes}
- Surrey changed most: strata rose from `r s_share(2005)`% of its sales in 2005 to `r s_share(2025)`% in 2025.
- A share chart does not say whether strata sales rose or single-family sales fell. Ask students which chart would tell them.
:::
